Ra. The sun god and supreme deity of ancient Egypt, worshipped throughout Egypt's three thousand years of history. Ra is the creative force and embodiment of cosmic order who journeys across the sky in his solar barque each day and battles chaos in the underworld each night. His daily renewal represents the victory of order over chaos and the legitimacy of pharaonic rule. Ra is typically depicted with a falcon head crowned with the solar disk, often wearing the sacred cobra, the uraeus, as a symbol of royal and divine authority. He was called by different names and forms at different times of day, encoding the fundamental Egyptian belief that reality is renewed each day through cosmic struggle. In the early morning, he appeared as Khepri, the scarab beetle, representing renewal and rebirth. At noon he was Ra in his full power and glory. As the sun descended at dusk, he became Atum, the aging god at the end of his journey. According to Egyptian belief, Ra existed from creation itself. In some versions he created himself through his own will. In others, he emerged from the primordial waters as the first god to exist. Ra's journey across the sky by day took place in his solar barque, a sacred boat pulled by divine power, bringing light and life to the world below. Each night, he journeyed through the Duat, the Egyptian underworld. This was a perilous passage through twelve regions, each representing one hour of darkness. During this nightly journey, Ra had to battle the serpent of chaos called Apophis, who sought to swallow him and prevent the sun's rebirth at dawn. The Egyptians believed that Ra's nightly victory over Apophis ensured the renewal of the world each dawn. They understood the sunrise not as a routine event but as a daily miracle achieved through cosmic struggle. Ra was the father of Shu, the god of air and wind, and Tefnut, the goddess of moisture. Their union produced Geb, the earth, and Nut, the sky. Ra created all the gods and all mortals, either through his conscious will or through divine emanation. Creation was not a single event but an ongoing process of renewal. All Egyptians believed themselves to be the cattle of Ra, dependent upon his daily creation and renewal for their continued existence. From the Fourth Dynasty onward, the pharaoh was considered the Son of Ra, linking royal authority directly to the supreme solar deity. This divine sonship meant the pharaoh was responsible for maintaining Ma'at, cosmic order, through proper ritual and governance, mirroring Ra's daily victory over chaos. During Egypt's New Kingdom, Ra was merged with Amon, the king of the gods, to become Amon-Ra, the chief god of the imperial pantheon. This merger combined Ra's solar power with Amon's hidden creative force. The heretic pharaoh Akhenaten challenged this tradition by elevating the solar disk Aten to supreme status, a theological revolution that lasted only one reign before being suppressed. Late in Egyptian history, Ra was sometimes syncretized with Osiris in the underworld, creating a complex theology where the sun god and the god of resurrection were identified as one. Ra's primary cult center was Heliopolis, the City of the Sun, which served as a major theological and political hub throughout Egyptian history. Daily offerings and rituals were performed to ensure Ra's continued strength and his victory over Apophis. The Egyptian priesthood saw themselves as cosmic guardians supporting the sun god's eternal work against chaos.
